cards.title: The same few parts
cards.body:
Phones, laptops, tablets and games consoles look very different on the outside. Inside, they're surprisingly alike: nearly all of them are built from the **same handful of parts**.

In this lesson you'll open up a laptop and a phone, find those parts, and learn what each one does.

cards.title: Before we open anything
cards.body:
Everything you take apart in this course is a **simulation**: tap and drag as much as you like.

Real phones and laptops are different. **Don't open one without an adult or a repair shop.** It can break parts, it can end the device's [[warranty]] (the maker's promise to fix it for free), and the **lithium battery inside can catch fire if it's bent or punctured**.

cards.prompt: Here's the inside of a laptop, with its bottom panel off. It's an example with a **removable** RAM stick and SSD: many thin laptops have them **soldered** to the board instead. **Tap each part** to find out what it is and what it does.

parts.job: The big board everything plugs into. Its thin lines carry signals between the parts, like roads.
The CPU, the brain. It follows the instructions that make apps work. A small shiny chip on a square base.
A copper tube that carries the CPU's heat away to metal fins by the vent. The copper pipe.
Blows air through the heat pipe's fins and out of the vents, so the CPU doesn't overheat. The round part with blades.
RAM: a fast workspace for whatever you're using right now. Here it's a stick with a row of chips, clipped into a slot.
The SSD keeps your photos, apps and files, even when the power is off. The long, narrow card with striped chips.
Stores the energy that runs everything. It's the biggest part: a row of flat cells with a lightning bolt.
Joins the battery to the board. Technicians unplug it first, so nothing gets power.

cards.explanation: Almost every laptop has these same parts. Remember the clues: the fan's blades, the copper heat pipe, the [[CPU]]'s small shiny chip, [[RAM]]'s row of chips, [[storage]]'s stripes and the battery's lightning bolt. (The bolt and stripes are this diagram's clues: real parts have printed labels instead.)

cards.title: Here's the inside of a real laptop

photo.alt: A real laptop with its bottom cover off: a round fan and a curved black heat pipe at the top, a long narrow SSD card in the middle, and a wide battery across the bottom.

cards.caption: A **Framework Laptop 13** (2023) with its bottom cover off. Find the fan, the curved heat pipe (black-coated in this one), the long, narrow SSD and the wide battery. This model lets you swap the RAM and SSD; in many thin laptops they're soldered to the board.

cards.prompt: Now open a laptop yourself. Take out the **four screws**, lift off the **bottom panel**, then **unplug the battery** before touching anything else. (Real laptops often have more screws, and clips too.)

actions.nudge: Unscrew this one first.
Unscrew this one first.
Unscrew this one first.
Unscrew this one first.
The panel won't lift until all four screws are out.
Lift the panel off first.

cards.explanation: Screws first, then the panel. Then technicians **unplug the battery** before they touch any other part, so nothing gets a jolt of power while they work.
cards.hint: Follow the order in the prompt. The panel is held on by screws, and the battery connector only shows once the panel is off.

cards.prompt: Here's the inside. Label the five main parts.
cards.explanation: The **battery** is the biggest part. The small shiny chip is the **CPU**, and the heat pipe carries its heat to the round **fan**. The stick with a row of chips is **RAM**, and the long, narrow card is **storage** (the SSD).
cards.hint: Use the clues from exploring: blades, a small shiny chip, a stick with a row of chips, a long card with striped chips, and a lightning bolt.
cards.nudge: Look again at the shapes. RAM is the stick with a row of chips in its slot; the SSD is the longer, narrower card with striped chips.

cards.prompt: Match each part to its job.
cards.explanation: The **CPU** does the work, **RAM** holds what's in use, **storage** keeps things for later, the **motherboard** links everything, and the **battery** powers it all.
cards.hint: Think back to what each part did when you tapped it inside the laptop. Start with the one you're surest of.
cards.nudge: RAM and storage are easy to mix up: one is a fast workspace for right now, the other keeps things when the power is off.

cards.prompt: A phone has the same jobs to do, squeezed into a much smaller space. **Tap each part** to meet it.

parts.job: The camera module. Its lens looks out through the back cover, and it plugs into the board with its own little cable.
The processor. It does the CPU's job and more (graphics too) in one chip. The small shiny chip on a square base.
A RAM chip: the fast workspace, soldered on so it can't be swapped. In many phones it sits right on top of the processor.
The storage chip keeps your photos, apps and messages, even when the phone is off. Soldered on too. It's marked with stripes.
Stores the energy. It fills most of the phone, so it can last all day. Look for the lightning bolt.
Joins the battery to the board. It's unplugged first in every repair.
A small metal bracket, held by two tiny screws, that stops the battery connector popping off.
Where the charger plugs in, in the middle of the bottom edge. It's open to the outside, so pocket fluff can get in.
Plays sounds and music. It's the small grille of holes near the bottom.
A tiny motor with an off-centre weight. It spins to make the phone buzz.

cards.explanation: Same jobs as the laptop, packed tighter: the processor, a [[RAM]] chip and a [[storage]] chip are all soldered to one small board, so none of them can be swapped. The battery takes up most of the space. Most phones have no fan.

cards.title: Here's the inside of a real phone

photo.alt: A real smartphone with its glued back removed: a large battery fills the middle, with metal plates covering the boards above and below it and the cameras at the top left.

cards.caption: A **Huawei P Smart Z** (2019) with its glued-on back removed. Just like in the diagram, the **battery** takes up most of the space. Its printed warning says: do not disassemble, puncture, crush, heat or burn.

cards.prompt: Now a phone. Phones are **glued shut**, so repairers soften the glue first. In this simulation: soften the glue, lift off the back, take out the **two tiny screws**, lift the **bracket**, then **unplug the battery**.

actions.nudge: Soften the glue on the back cover first.
The glue is still hard. Soften it first.
Take the back cover off first.
Take the back cover off first.
Both tiny screws have to come out first.
Lift the bracket off the connector first.

cards.explanation: Soften the glue, lift the back, take out the bracket's screws and the bracket, then **unplug the battery** before touching anything else. Repair shops do this with special tools and training, because a damaged phone battery can catch fire.
cards.hint: Follow the order in the prompt. The back won't lift until its glue is soft, and a bracket holds the battery connector down.
cards.safety: **Heating or prying a phone can damage its battery and start a fire.** That's why repair shops use special tools and training. It's never something to try at home.

cards.prompt: Tap the part where this phone keeps your **photos**, even when it's switched off.
cards.explanation: Photos live in **storage**, which keeps everything when the power is off. RAM only holds what's in use right now, and forgets it all when the phone turns off.
cards.hint: Your photos have to survive the phone being switched off. Which part keeps things when the power goes?
cards.nudge: The camera takes photos, but it doesn't keep them, and [[RAM]] forgets everything when the phone turns off. Which part keeps your files for good?

cards.prompt: Label the phone's parts. They're smaller and packed tighter than the laptop's.
cards.explanation: A phone squeezes the **processor**, **RAM** and **storage** chips onto one small board at the top, with the **camera** beside them. The **battery** takes up most of the space, because it has to last all day.
cards.hint: The same clues work here, just smaller: a small shiny chip, a chip of little squares, stripes and a lightning bolt. The camera sits beside the main chips.
cards.nudge: The main chips are packed close together. Check each one's look: the shiny chip on its base, the chip of little squares, and the stripes.

cards.prompt: A repair: take the camera out, fit it back in, then close the phone up again in a safe order.

actions.nudge: Soften the glue on the back cover first.
The glue is still hard. Soften it first.
Take the back cover off first.
Take the back cover off first.
Both tiny screws have to come out first.
Lift the bracket off the connector first.
Unplug the battery before touching any other part.
Take the old camera out first.
Fit the camera back before reconnecting the battery.
Reconnect the battery before the bracket goes back.
Put the bracket back first.
Put the bracket back first.
Screw the bracket down before closing the phone.

cards.explanation: Putting a device back together is taking it apart in reverse. The battery is **unplugged first** and **plugged back in last**, then the bracket, its screws and the back go on. (Real repairers also fit new glue and test the phone before closing it.)
cards.hint: Open it the way you did before. Parts you take out wait in the **Parts out** tray: tap one there to fit it back. Close up in reverse order: battery, bracket, screws, then the back.
cards.safety: **Heating or prying a phone can damage its battery and start a fire.** That's why repair shops use special tools and training. It's never something to try at home.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Phones and laptops are built from the same parts: **CPU**, **RAM**, **storage**, a **battery**, and the **motherboard** that connects them.
- The CPU does the work, RAM holds what's in use now, and storage keeps things for later.
- In phones, the RAM and storage are chips **soldered** to the board. Some laptops let you swap the RAM and SSD; many thin ones don't.
- Technicians **unplug the battery first** and plug it back in last.
- Real devices should only be opened by an adult or a repair shop.

Next: why RAM and storage are so different.
